title: Korean & Japanese Hangover Pills: Condition, Dawn 808, Ukon no Chikara
excerpt: What is really inside Korean hangover drinks (Condition, Morning Care, Dawn 808) and Japanese ones (Ukon no Chikara, Hepalyse), what the evidence says, safety, and where to buy them in the US.
metaDescription: Condition, Morning Care, Dawn 808, Ukon no Chikara and Hepalyse: what's inside, what the evidence says, safety, and where to buy them in the US.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the famous Korean and Japanese hangover products are built on two plant ingredients. Korean brands like Condition and Morning Care lean on **hovenia** (the Japanese raisin tree, called *heotgae* in Korean), the same plant that gave the world DHM. Japan's best-known option, Ukon no Chikara, is built on **turmeric (curcumin)**, while Hepalyse is built mainly on a **liver extract** plus vitamins. All of them are widely used and mostly low-risk for healthy adults, but the human evidence behind them is thin: a handful of small studies, many of them run with or for the companies that make the products. None of them stops you from getting drunk, and none of them protects you from the long-term harms of heavy drinking.

**The quick take:** If you're curious, these drinks and pills are a reasonable thing to try alongside water, food, and pacing, not instead of them. Hovenia-based products have the most plausible story, because the plant contains DHM, which has real (though mostly animal) research behind it. Turmeric-based products have a weaker hangover case. If you flush red when you drink, none of these products fixes the underlying gene, so please read the section on Asian flush before relying on them.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research and product information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using these products if** you take blood thinners, diabetes medicine, or other daily prescriptions, if you have liver or gallbladder disease, if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or if you drink heavily most days. Imported products are not reviewed by the FDA for safety or effectiveness. If someone has had a dangerous amount of alcohol (confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or they can't be woken), call 911.

## Why Korea and Japan Have a Whole Hangover Industry

In South Korea and Japan, after-work drinking with colleagues has long been part of business culture, and a large market has grown around helping people get through the next morning. In Korea these products are usually called *haejang* (hangover-relief) drinks, and they sit next to the register in almost every convenience store. In Japan, small bottled "energy" and liver drinks line the shelves of convenience stores and drugstores, and many people drink one before a night out.

The category matters for two reasons. First, it popularized the idea of taking something *before* drinking, which is the opposite of the Western "cure it in the morning" habit. Second, it put hovenia in front of millions of people decades before DHM supplements showed up on Amazon. If you've read our [complete guide to DHM and the Japanese raisin tree](/never-hungover/dhm-japanese-raisin-tree-complete-guide), you already know the plant. These products are where many people first meet it.

## The Korean Products: Condition, Morning Care, and Dawn 808

Korean hangover products come mostly as small drinks (around the size of an energy shot), with newer pill, jelly-stick, and chewable versions. Formulas change over time and vary between versions of the same brand, so always read the current label. Here's what the three best-known brands are built around.

### Condition (컨디션)

Condition is the brand most people mean when they talk about Korean hangover drinks. It has been on the market since the early 1990s, originally from CJ's pharmaceutical arm and now sold by HK inno.N. The core ingredient across the line is **hovenia extract** (*heotgae*), usually from the fruit or fruit stalks of *Hovenia dulcis*. Different versions add other ingredients such as plant extracts, amino acids, or sweeteners, and there are spin-offs aimed at specific groups (for example, a version marketed to women) and in different formats, including small pills and jelly sticks.

**What to expect:** a sweet, slightly herbal shot. Most people take it before or during drinking. The label typically doesn't tell you how much DHM is in the hovenia extract, so you can't compare it directly to a DHM supplement.

### Morning Care (모닝케어)

Morning Care comes from Dong-A Pharmaceutical. Like Condition, the line is built around **hovenia**, with various versions adding other herbal extracts. It's sold in the same convenience-store format and is one of Condition's main competitors in Korea.

**What to expect:** very similar use and experience to Condition. The differences between the two are mostly about flavor, format, and the secondary ingredients, not a different mechanism.

### Dawn 808 (여명808)

Dawn 808 (*Yeomyeong* 808) is made by a company called Glami and is known for a long list of herbal ingredients rather than a single headline extract. The company's marketing has long leaned on the number of ingredients and on its development story. The exact formula is proprietary, and with that many components, it's hard to know which ones, if any, are doing the work.

**What to expect:** a stronger, more medicinal taste than Condition or Morning Care, and a reputation among fans as the "serious" option. That reputation comes from word of mouth and marketing, not from head-to-head trials.

### Other Korean options you'll see

- **Korean pear juice** drinks (*bae* juice), often sold as a hangover remedy. Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, presented early findings about Korean pear juice and hangovers in 2013, but that was a small study and it was never a large, independent trial.
- **Hovenia tea** and hovenia water, which are less concentrated than the branded shots.
- Pill and chewable formats of the major brands, which are easier to carry and to import.

## The Japanese Products: Ukon no Chikara and Hepalyse

Japanese products split into two families: turmeric drinks and liver-support drinks. They're sold in convenience stores and drugstores, and some versions are regulated more like medicines than foods in Japan.

### Ukon no Chikara (ウコンの力)

*Ukon* is the Japanese word for turmeric, and *Ukon no Chikara* means "the power of turmeric." Made by House Wellness Foods, it's a small bottled drink containing **turmeric extract with curcumin**, the yellow compound in turmeric that most research focuses on. It also comes in granule and tablet forms. In Japan it's common to drink one before a night out.

**What to expect:** a small, slightly bitter, fruity drink. The brand has used more absorbable forms of curcumin in some versions, which matters because plain curcumin is poorly absorbed by the body.

### Hepalyse (ヘパリーゼ)

Hepalyse is made by Zeria Pharmaceutical. Its main ingredient is **liver hydrolysate**, a processed extract made from animal liver, combined with B vitamins and, in some versions, other ingredients. It's sold as a drink and in tablet form, and the line includes several versions with different regulatory status in Japan, from food-like products to over-the-counter medicines.

**What to expect:** a vitamin-drink style taste. Because the core ingredient comes from animal liver, Hepalyse may not suit vegetarians, vegans, or people who avoid certain animal products for religious reasons. Check the source animal on the current label.

### Other Japanese options

You'll also see products like Taisho's Solmac (more of a stomach-settling product) and generic turmeric drinks from other companies. The turmeric category is much bigger than any one brand.

## What's Actually Inside: The Key Ingredients Explained

### Hovenia (Japanese raisin tree, *heotgae*)

*Hovenia dulcis* is a tree native to East Asia. Its fruit stalks have been used in traditional Chinese, Korean, and Japanese medicine for hangovers for centuries. The modern interest comes from **dihydromyricetin (DHM)**, a flavonoid found in hovenia and in a few other plants.

The best-known DHM study is a 2012 paper by Shen and colleagues in the *Journal of Neuroscience*. In rats, DHM reduced alcohol intoxication and some withdrawal effects, and the researchers linked this to how DHM affects GABA-A receptors in the brain, the same receptors alcohol acts on. Other animal and lab research suggests DHM may support how the liver handles alcohol and its toxic by-product, acetaldehyde. We explain this in more depth in our [DHM science explainer](/never-hungover/dhm-science-explained).

Here is the important caveat. **The human side is much weaker.** There are a few small Korean human studies on hovenia extract and hangover symptoms, and the results have been encouraging but far from conclusive. Many involve small groups, short follow-up, and industry ties. Also, a branded drink lists "hovenia extract," not a DHM dose, so you can't tell how much DHM you're getting.

### Turmeric and curcumin

Curcumin has been studied for inflammation and liver health for years, mostly in lab and animal research. Its big practical problem is absorption: plain curcumin is poorly absorbed and quickly cleared. That's why manufacturers use specially processed forms.

For hangovers specifically, the evidence is weak. A small Japanese study published in 2011 tested a highly absorbable curcumin formulation and reported lower blood acetaldehyde after drinking in a handful of volunteers. That's interesting, but it's a tiny study of one specific formulation, and it doesn't prove that a turmeric drink makes you feel better the next morning. Turmeric products are not a well-tested hangover treatment.

### Liver hydrolysate (Hepalyse)

Liver hydrolysate is a long-used ingredient in Japanese tonics. The research behind it, as it relates to hangovers, is mostly from Japan, and much of it is small or connected to manufacturers. We're not aware of strong, independent trials showing it reduces hangover symptoms. The B vitamins in these drinks are useful if you're actually low in them, which heavy drinkers sometimes are, but they won't undo a night of drinking.

### The supporting cast

Many of these drinks also contain sugar or sweeteners, amino acids, other plant extracts, and sometimes caffeine. A sugary drink and a bit of fluid can make you feel slightly better on their own, which makes it hard to tell what the "active" ingredient is doing.

## What Does the Research Say About These Products Overall?

The best way to judge any hangover remedy is to look at systematic reviews, which pull together all the trials on a topic and rate their quality.

- In 2005, a systematic review in the *BMJ* by Pittler, Verster, and Ernst looked at randomized trials of hangover remedies and concluded there was no compelling evidence that any of them worked.
- In 2022, a systematic review in the journal *Addiction* by Roberts and colleagues revisited the field. It found that a few remedies, including hovenia fruit extract and Korean pear juice, showed some signs of benefit in individual studies, but rated the overall quality of the evidence as very low. The authors called for larger, better-designed trials.

So the fair summary is: **hovenia has a plausible mechanism and some early human data, turmeric and liver extract have less, and there is no good evidence from large independent trials that anything in this category prevents hangovers.** That's not a reason to avoid them entirely. It's a reason to keep expectations modest and not drink more because you've taken one.

## How These Products Compare

| Product | Country | Main ingredient | Typical format | Strength of hangover evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Condition | Korea | Hovenia extract | Drink, pill, jelly stick | Limited (plausible, small studies on hovenia) |
| Morning Care | Korea | Hovenia extract plus herbs | Drink, pill | Limited (same as above) |
| Dawn 808 | Korea | Multi-herb blend | Drink | Very limited (proprietary mix) |
| Ukon no Chikara | Japan | Turmeric / curcumin | Drink, granules, tablets | Very limited (tiny studies) |
| Hepalyse | Japan | Liver hydrolysate plus B vitamins | Drink, tablets | Very limited (mostly manufacturer data) |
| DHM supplement | US and elsewhere | DHM (labeled dose) | Capsule | Limited (mostly animal research, few human studies) |

The last row is there for a reason. If what draws you to Condition or Morning Care is hovenia, a DHM supplement gives you the compound researchers are most interested in, at a dose printed on the label, without the sugar.

## If You Get Asian Flush, Read This First

Many people who look up Korean and Japanese hangover products are dealing with **alcohol flush reaction**: red face, fast heartbeat, and feeling unwell after a small amount of alcohol. It's common in people of East Asian descent and is mostly caused by a variant in the **ALDH2** gene. That variant makes the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde work poorly, so acetaldehyde, a toxic and cancer-causing by-product of alcohol, builds up.

This matters for three reasons:

1. **No hangover drink fixes the gene.** Some products claim to help clear acetaldehyde, but they don't restore ALDH2 function. You'll still be exposed to more acetaldehyde than someone without the variant.
2. **Hiding the flush can be dangerous.** Research has linked the flushing response to a higher risk of esophageal cancer in people who drink regularly. A widely cited 2009 paper by Brooks and colleagues in *PLOS Medicine* described the flush as an unrecognized warning sign for that risk. Masking the symptom (for example with antihistamines) while continuing to drink doesn't reduce the underlying risk.
3. **The safest approach is drinking less.** If you flush, the most effective way to protect yourself is to drink less, and less often.

Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) goes through the genetics, the risks, and what helps in much more detail.

## Safety: Who Should Be Careful

These products are sold over the counter and are mostly low-risk for healthy adults at label doses, but that doesn't make them risk-free.

- **Turmeric and the liver.** Turmeric supplements, especially concentrated, highly absorbable forms, have been linked to rare cases of liver injury. In 2019, Italian health authorities investigated a cluster of hepatitis cases in people taking turmeric supplements. Stop and see a doctor if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs.
- **Turmeric and medications.** Curcumin may add to the effect of blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs and may interact with some diabetes medicines. People with gallstones or gallbladder disease are often advised to avoid concentrated turmeric.
- **Hovenia and DHM interactions.** Data are limited. If you take daily prescription medicines, particularly ones processed by the liver, ask a pharmacist. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers the main questions.
- **Animal-derived ingredients.** Hepalyse's liver hydrolysate comes from animal liver. Check the label if you avoid particular animal products.
- **Sugar and caffeine.** Some drinks contain a fair amount of sugar, and some contain caffeine. That's worth knowing if you have diabetes or are sensitive to caffeine.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding.** There's no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy, and these products haven't been studied for safety in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
- **Regular heavy drinking.** If you need a hangover product most mornings, that's a sign to talk to a doctor about your drinking, not to find a better product. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is free and confidential.

## Where to Buy Korean and Japanese Hangover Products in the US

These products aren't stocked by most US pharmacies, but they're not hard to find.

- **Korean grocery chains** such as H Mart often carry Condition, Morning Care, and Dawn 808, usually near the checkout or in the drinks section. Smaller Korean markets often carry them too.
- **Japanese grocery stores** such as Mitsuwa and other Japanese markets sometimes carry Ukon no Chikara and other turmeric drinks. Hepalyse is less common.
- **Online marketplaces** like Amazon and eBay have third-party sellers who import these products, and some Asian grocery delivery services carry them.

A few cautions when buying imports:

- **Check the expiration date.** Imported drinks can sit in warehouses for a long time.
- **Labels may be only in Korean or Japanese.** Use a translation app to check ingredients and allergens, or buy from a seller who provides an English ingredient list.
- **Look out for fakes and gray-market stock.** Buy from established grocery chains or sellers with a long track record and plenty of reviews.
- **Regulatory status varies.** Some Japanese versions are classified as medicines in Japan, and imported products are not reviewed by the FDA. Personal-use imports and resale rules differ by product.
- **Price.** Expect to pay noticeably more per bottle in the US than in Seoul or Tokyo, because of import costs.

## Should You Try Them?

**Reasons you might:**

- They're widely used, easy to take, and mostly well tolerated.
- Hovenia-based products contain the plant that DHM research is based on.
- Taking something before drinking can be a useful reminder to plan the night: eat first, pace yourself, and alternate with water.

**Reasons to be skeptical:**

- The evidence is small and often industry-linked.
- Branded drinks rarely tell you how much of the key compound you're getting.
- Turmeric concentrates carry a small but real liver-injury risk.
- They're expensive and harder to find in the US.

**A practical alternative:** if the hovenia story is what interests you, a DHM supplement is the closer and more transparent option. In our testing and reviews, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a straightforward single-ingredient choice with the dose on the label, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it. We want to be straight with you: DHM's human evidence is also limited, and it won't make heavy drinking safe. It's one tool, not a shield.

## What Actually Helps Most

Whatever you take, the basics still do most of the work:

- **Drink less, and more slowly.** The amount of alcohol is the biggest driver of a hangover.
- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Alternate with water.** It won't cure a hangover, but it helps with thirst and headache.
- **Choose clearer drinks.** Darker drinks like whiskey and red wine contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation that may make hangovers worse.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, and poor sleep makes the next day feel worse.

For a full plan, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover), and if you're comparing liver-support options, our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) covers the ingredients with the best evidence. If you're also curious about other popular products, our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) and [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) guide look at the alternatives honestly.

## The Bottom Line

Korean hangover drinks like Condition, Morning Care, and Dawn 808 are built mostly on hovenia, the plant behind DHM. Japanese options like Ukon no Chikara rely on turmeric, and Hepalyse relies on liver extract and vitamins. All are popular and generally low-risk for healthy adults, but the evidence that they prevent hangovers is limited and mostly small-scale. Hovenia has the most plausible case. If you flush when you drink, none of these products fixes the underlying problem, and drinking less is the only real protection. Buy from reputable Korean or Japanese grocers, check labels and expiration dates, and talk to a pharmacist if you take daily medications.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do Korean hangover drinks like Condition actually work?**

They may help a little, but the evidence is limited. Condition and Morning Care are built on hovenia extract, which contains DHM. DHM has promising animal research, and a few small Korean human studies on hovenia have reported fewer hangover symptoms, but a 2022 systematic review in the journal Addiction rated the overall quality of hangover-remedy evidence as very low. Treat them as a modest helper alongside water, food, and pacing, not as a guarantee.

**What is the main ingredient in Korean hangover cures?**

Most Korean hangover drinks, including Condition and Morning Care, are built around hovenia (Hovenia dulcis), known in Korean as heotgae and in English as the Japanese raisin tree. Dawn 808 uses a longer blend of herbal extracts. Many versions also contain sugar, amino acids, and other plant extracts. Formulas change, so check the current label.

**Does Ukon no Chikara (turmeric) prevent hangovers?**

There's very little evidence that it does. Ukon no Chikara contains turmeric extract with curcumin. A small Japanese study reported lower blood acetaldehyde after drinking with a highly absorbable curcumin formulation, but that's a tiny study and doesn't show people actually feel better the next day. Concentrated turmeric has also been linked to rare cases of liver injury and may interact with blood thinners.

**What is in Hepalyse?**

Hepalyse, made by Zeria Pharmaceutical in Japan, is built mainly on liver hydrolysate, an extract made from animal liver, plus B vitamins and, in some versions, other ingredients. The evidence that it reduces hangover symptoms is mostly small and manufacturer-linked. Because the core ingredient is animal-derived, check the label if you avoid certain animal products.

**Where can I buy Korean and Japanese hangover drinks in the US?**

Korean grocery chains like H Mart often carry Condition, Morning Care, and Dawn 808. Japanese markets such as Mitsuwa sometimes carry Ukon no Chikara. You can also find them from third-party sellers on Amazon and eBay. Buy from established stores or sellers, check the expiration date, and translate the ingredient list if it's only in Korean or Japanese.

**Do Korean or Japanese hangover drinks help with Asian flush?**

No. Asian flush is mostly caused by a variant in the ALDH2 gene that makes it hard to clear acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. No hangover drink restores that enzyme. Research has linked the flush to a higher risk of esophageal cancer in people who drink regularly, so masking it while continuing to drink doesn't make drinking safer. Drinking less is the most effective protection.

**Is a DHM supplement the same as a Korean hovenia drink?**

Not exactly. Hovenia drinks contain hovenia extract, which includes DHM along with other compounds, but the label usually doesn't say how much DHM you're getting. A DHM supplement lists the dose directly and doesn't add sugar. Both share the same limitation: most DHM research is in animals, and human evidence is still limited.

**Are Korean and Japanese hangover products safe?**

For most healthy adults at label doses, they appear to be low-risk. Be more careful if you take blood thinners or diabetes medicine, have liver or gallbladder disease, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or drink heavily most days. Imported products are not reviewed by the FDA, so talk to a doctor or pharmacist if you have health conditions or take daily medications.
